items.title: Houthi Strike on Saudi Airport Kills 2 as U.S. Tells Some Diplomats to Leave
items.summary: The airport is in Dammam, which is near the headquarters of oil giant Saudi Aramco. For weeks, Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi militia has been attacking the kingdom’s aviation and energy sectors.
items.full_text:
Title: Houthi Strike on Saudi Airport Kills 2 as U.S. Tells Some Diplomats to Leave - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/22/world/middleeast/saudi-houthis-yemen-dammam-airport.html

Published Time: Thu, 22 Oct 2026 19:00:32 GMT

Markdown Content:
At least two people were killed in a strike by the Iran-backed Houthi militia on a major airport in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, as Washington ordered some U.S. diplomatic staff to leave the kingdom following weeks of deadly attacks.

The Saudi authorities said in a statement on Thursday morning that a Saudi national and an Indian resident died in the strike on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, a city in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province that is home to the state oil giant Saudi Aramco. Eight other people were wounded, the statement said, adding that airport was operating normally on Thursday.

A spokesman for Yemen’s Houthis, Yahya Saree, said on Thursday that the militia had targeted Dammam’s airport. He also said, in the same statement, that the Houthis had targeted the Saudi defense ministry in the capital, Riyadh, along with an Aramco site in Yanbu, and an airport in the southern city of Abha. The Saudi authorities have not commented on those claims.

In a separate incident, two people were killed and two others were wounded on Wednesday when a drone was intercepted over Aramco’s Shaybah oil field, also in the Eastern Province. Falling drone fragments sparked a fire in a contractor’s vehicle, killing a Filipino and a Nepali, the [Saudi Energy Ministry said](https://x.com/MoEnergy_Saudi/status/2113004532045103144/photo/1).

The Houthis have been pummeling Saudi Arabia’s aviation and energy infrastructure for weeks, killing at least 22 civilians and roiling energy markets.

The price of oil jumped about 3 percent on Thursday, with the global benchmark topping $112 a barrel, the highest level since mid-May.

Saudi Aramco staff were instructed to leave the company’s headquarters building in Dhahran and to work remotely on Thursday, according to two people familiar with the situation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak for the company. Aramco did not respond to a request for comment and the Saudi energy ministry referred questions to Aramco.

Saudi Arabia announced a [bombing campaign against the Houthis this month](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/world/middleeast/saudi-arabia-yemen-houthis-bab-al-mandab-strait.html) in support of the internationally recognized government of Yemen, which has been at war with the Houthis since 2014. That was when the Houthis, a rebel group from the country’s north, seized the Yemeni capital, Sanaa — which they still hold.

A fragile truce in Yemen unraveled earlier this year, and the country has since tipped back into a civil war that the United Nations says has displaced some 260,000 people since August. [At least 1,574 people have been killed](https://www.emro.who.int/yemen/information-resources/yemen-conflict-escalation-situation-report.html) since then, the World Health Organization said this week.

As the fighting has spilled onto Saudi soil, the United States ordered all “non-emergency government employees and their family members” to leave Saudi Arabia, a State Department spokesman, Tommy Pigott, said [in a social media](https://x.com/statedeptspox/status/2112988488379273237) post on Wednesday night that cited the Houthis’ attacks, mounting civilian casualties and travel disruptions.

Washington had pulled many diplomatic staff out of the Middle East earlier this year after the start of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, the Houthis’ main patron. But it [started sending some back](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/25/world/middleeast/us-diplomats-middle-east-embassies.html) in late August.

Then in September, the Houthis seized areas of strategic territory on Yemen’s Red Sea coast in a [lightning offensive](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/06/world/middleeast/yemen-houthis-reconstruct.html), gaining greater control over a crucial choke point for global trade. In recent weeks, forces affiliated with the Yemeni government and backed by Saudi warplanes have mounted a counteroffensive to retake the territory.

The Red Sea has become an increasingly important route for Saudi oil exports since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway in the Persian Gulf, after the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February. The Houthis’ attacks on Saudi oil facilities and tankers traversing the Red Sea have heaped further pressure on energy markets.

Some ships continue to transit the Strait of Hormuz, despite the risks. In the meantime, regional mediators have been trying to negotiate an end to the U.S. war with Iran and a reopening of the waterway.

The U.S. and Israeli militaries have [developed plans for renewed strikes](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/21/us/politics/us-israel-renewed-iran-strikes.html) against Iran after next month’s American midterm elections, according to U.S. officials and other people briefed on the deliberations.

President Trump said on Wednesday that Washington was not currently negotiating with Iran and “something one way or the other” will happen “fairly soon.”

Iranian attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have ramped up in recent weeks. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said on Thursday that it had struck four tankers in the northern Persian Gulf that it claimed had been illegally transferring oil. It also said that three more vessels had hit mines in the western Strait of Hormuz. Those attacks could not immediately be independently confirmed.

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen, Saeed Al-Batati from al-Mukalla, Yemen and Lisa Friedman and Sanam Mahoozi from London.

items.title: As Typhoon Champi Nears, Taiwan’s Mayors Bet on a Popular Day Off
items.summary: One expert said the likelihood that a mayor announces closure of work and school because of a typhoon increases 31 percent during an election year.
items.full_text:
Title: As Typhoon Champi Nears, Taiwan’s Mayors Bet on a Popular Day Off - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/22/world/asia/taiwan-typhoon-champi-mayors.html

Published Time: Thu, 22 Oct 2026 19:11:56 GMT

Markdown Content:
In Taiwan, typhoons are not just tropical storms that cause flooding and damage. They can make or break a mayor’s chance at re-election for reasons one might not expect.

Several times a year between summer and fall, when the subtropical island is hit by cyclones, city and county mayors must decide whether to order a “typhoon day off,” when government offices, schools and most businesses will close.

Taiwan has been bracing for Typhoon Champi, which was at one point a super typhoon and the [strongest storm of 2026](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/21/weather/super-typhoon-champi-strongest-storm-year.html). On Thursday, the mayor of Taipei, Chiang Wan-an, called a typhoon day off for Friday, and urged residents to be careful. The storm is expected to pass the northeastern part of Taiwan, bringing heavy rain and winds of 141 miles per hour.

The decision did not come as a surprise to many, not least because of the weather forecast. Mr. Chiang faces re-election in late November, and typhoon days are popular with residents, who often spend the day at home. If the storm turns out to be weaker than forecast, many go shopping, to the movies or to sing karaoke. (Mr. Chiang, a member of the Nationalist Party, also called the Kuomintang, is in a close race with Puma Shen, a popular legislator from the governing Democratic Progressive Party.)

Almost all cities and counties across Taiwan’s main island had suspended work and class on Friday.

Because typhoons are such a common part of daily life in Taiwan, decisions like whether or not to call a typhoon day matter to voters. Between 2001 and 2023, Taipei had [40 typhoon days off](https://www.thenewslens.com/article/190034), an average of almost two days a year, according to The News Lens, a local publication. Other cities like Yilan on the northeastern coast, which is often hit badly by storms, had 45 days off in that period.

According to Austin Wang, an associate professor at the University of Nevada who has studied the electoral politics of typhoon days, the likelihood that a mayor announces closure of work and school increases 31 percent during an election year.

Unlike other policies that can take months or years to evaluate, he said, it is clear within a day or two whether an official made the correct call. For instance, if a typhoon day is called and the storm turns out to be severe, the official made the right decision. The fact that the mayor’s office alone determines whether to call a day off also means that the decision is entirely the mayor’s responsibility.

“It is a very easy criteria for people to evaluate whether their incumbent was doing a good job or a bad job,” Mr. Wang said. When it comes to re-election, he said, “people will remember if the mayor made the right or wrong decision.”

Tickets for many high-speed trains leaving Taipei during working hours on Friday were fully or almost fully booked on Thursday. Supermarkets stocked extra supplies of water, produce and instant noodles, a common staple during typhoons.

On social media, residents discussed their plans to spend the four-day weekend binge watching television shows and sleeping. (Monday is a public holiday in Taiwan.) Earlier in the day, residents left comments on Mr. Chiang’s Facebook page, asking him to announce a day off.

Despite the popularity of such days, unnecessarily calling one can come back to haunt a candidate. Business groups often oppose typhoon days off because of the cost to companies, most of which still pay their employees for the day. Taiwan’s stock market also closes for the day if work and school are suspended in Taipei.

In July, when Typhoon Bavi approached Taiwan, Mr. Chiang ordered a day off on a Friday for residents to prepare for the storm’s arrival on the weekend. Commentators and his political rivals accused him of inventing the concept of a “typhoon preparation day” just to pander to voters.

But not calling one quickly enough may be even worse. When Typhoon Mikra passed over central Taiwan in June, the mayors of the city of Hsinchu and the county of Hsinchu, home to Taiwan’s largest semiconductor companies, were criticized for not issuing a typhoon day off. The next day, as the storm arrived, the county mayor, Yang Wenke, issued an apology and announced the suspension of work and school. That storm left two people dead.

Lai Ching-te, the president of Taiwan, has been both praised and derided for his weather-related decisions. In 2012, when Typhoon Tembin approached the southern city of Tainan, Mr. Lai, then that city’s mayor, decided it would be business as usual.

When the storm proved to be light, he earned the nickname “God Lai.”

But the next year, when once again he resisted pressure to declare a day off during another typhoon, the storm caused severe flooding in his city. He issued a public apology.

items.title: Employers Shift Rising Health Care Costs Onto Millions of Workers
items.summary: New surveys show that increases in premiums and deductibles are forcing people to forgo treatments or doctor’s visits while budgets are strained by higher food and gas prices.
items.full_text:
Title: Employers Shift Rising Health Care Costs Onto Millions of Workers - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/22/business/health-insurance-costs-workers-premiums-deductibles.html

Published Time: Thu, 22 Oct 2026 19:32:14 GMT

Markdown Content:
Working families are paying much more for health insurance this year, with many postponing doctor’s visits, treatments or filling prescriptions. The number of uninsured Americans is rising as more people wrestle with unpaid medical bills.

This is the stark picture emerging from two surveys released Thursday that show how millions of people in the United States are struggling to keep up with sharply climbing [medical costs](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/02/business/health-insurance-increases.html) in recent years.

As the [midterm elections approach](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/business/midterms-election-trump-drug-prices-affordability.html), Americans are ranking health care near or at the top of their financial concerns, according to [a recent poll](https://www.kff.org/public-opinion/kff-health-tracking-poll-public-views-on-fraud-in-government-health-programs/) from KFF, a nonprofit health research group.

Roughly six in 10 adults reported they were very or somewhat worried about affording care.

The majority of Americans — about 157 million — get insurance through their employer. But as costs for coverage have spiked, with increases in the high single digits, businesses have been shifting much more of the additional expenses onto their workforces.

Employees are paying more for coverage, especially if they work for a small business, according to KFF, which released its [annual survey of employers](https://www.kff.org/health-costs/2026-employer-health-benefits-survey/) about their health benefits.

Many people are also paying thousands of dollars in medical expenses when they get sick, because companies have increased the plans’ deductibles to offset increases in premiums.

The yearly price, on average, for employees to cover their family is now $7,471 a year, up 9 percent from 2025. The total cost for a family plan, including the amount the employer contributes to the annual premiums, has reached $28,303.

Overall, the average deductible for U.S. workers is approaching $2,000 before insurance kicks in, according to the survey.

“People tell us in polls that their health care costs are their top cost-of-living concern, tied with gas prices. The fact that workers’ share of premiums went up almost three times faster than inflation in 2026 helps explain why,” said Drew Altman, the president and chief executive of KFF, in an email.

Harder hit are employees of small companies, defined as those with fewer than 200 workers, whose paychecks have been shrinking as premiums increase, according to the KFF survey. On average, they are paying $9,687 a year for coverage.

More than a third of people working at a small employer have annual deductibles of $3,000 or more.

Companies are also erecting new hurdles for workers to get care, like cumbersome approval processes for expensive drugs or treatments, the KFF survey found. Another way that businesses are trying to lower costs has been to restrict employees’ choices of doctors or hospitals.

“Employers are paying the equivalent of buying an economy car for each employee who has family health insurance coverage, and in 2026 they offloaded more of that cost to workers,” Mr. Altman said. KFF surveyed more than 1,900 employers with at least 10 workers.

For their part, employers attribute higher costs to several factors, including hospital care, expensive new cancer therapies and expanding coverage of GLP-1 medications for obesity and diabetes.

The rollbacks in government programs like Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act have also left more people without health coverage, according to [a separate survey](https://www.commonwealthfund.org/user/media-login?destination=/publications/surveys/2026/oct/state-health-insurance-coverage-2026-biennial-survey) from the Commonwealth Fund, a nonprofit research foundation that analyzes Americans’ experience with insurance every other year. The fund has been a longtime supporter of the A.C.A. and other efforts to expand coverage.

The share of working-age adults who are uninsured rose to 11.2 percent in 2026 from 8.9 percent in 2024, the Commonwealth study showed. Conducted from early May through mid-July, the study has provided one of the first indications of whether people no longer enrolled in Medicaid and Obamacare found other sources of insurance.

The increase in the uninsured rate over the last two years “was really notable,” said Sara R. Collins, a senior scholar at the fund who led the Commonwealth research.

After Obamacare was enacted in 2010, the number of working-age adults and children without insurance [fell](https://www.kff.org/uninsured/key-facts-about-the-uninsured-population/?entry=trends-in-the-uninsured-population-uninsured-trends) from around 46 million to a low of about 25 million three years ago. The government changes and soaring medical costs across the broader health sector have fueled a backslide in coverage, bringing the estimated number this year to 30 million uninsured, according to the Congressional Budget Office.

The Trump administration is expected to release official figures on the number of uninsured Americans next year.

The recent increase is statistically significant, Ms. Collins said, and the previous Commonwealth estimates of the uninsured rate have been lower than the official government figures and generally tracked in the same direction.

The Commonwealth survey also noted that about 12 percent of working-age adults reported a gap or lapse in their insurance, the same share as in 2022.

The increase in the uninsured rate was not unexpected, with [some estimates](https://www.kff.org/affordable-care-act/individual-market-enrollment-continues-to-fall-through-mid-2026/) showing that nearly five million people dropped their individual coverage. Many were no longer able to afford their Obamacare insurance after President Trump and Republican lawmakers declined to extend pandemic-era subsidies that had helped defray the cost of a typical plan.

Enrollment in Medicaid, the federal-state program for the poor, has also been declining, although the bulk of the cuts to that program as part of Mr. Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act do not take place until next year. Over the last four years, the share of working-age adults enrolled in Medicaid dropped from 15.5 percent to 13 percent, according to Commonwealth.

But the Commonwealth survey, which was based on telephone and online interviews among a sample of 9,360 adults, also underscored how financially insecure people have become about their ability to pay for medical care. The number of people who said they had delayed or skipped care altogether because of the expense increased to 50 percent this year from 46 percent in 2022, according to the survey.

“These reports show the reason why health care costs are at the top of voter concern and outrage,” said Anthony Wright, the executive director of Families USA, a left-leaning consumer advocacy group.

The deepening strains on household budgets are also evident as the rate of medical debt or unpaid bills keeps rising, affecting even those who are insured. About a third of adults with individual policies and those with coverage from an employer reported they were paying off medical bills or medical debt they had already incurred, according to the Commonwealth Fund.

People without insurance tend to have lower levels of medical debt, Ms. Collins of Commonwealth said. “You just use less care if you don’t have insurance coverage.”

The survey found that most Americans believed the federal government had a responsibility to ensure that people had coverage, although Democrats and independents expressed that belief more strongly than Republicans.

“They are mad at hospitals and drug companies and insurers for charging so much,” said Mr. Wright of Families USA. “They are furious at Congress for not reining them in.”

Employers and insurers “have never addressed, not in a significant way, the drivers of health care costs,” Ms. Collins said. “Health care costs are the thing that drives premiums and deductibles.”
